It was also said: it is from their attributing to Him a son, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The heavens are almost torn apart from it﴾.

If you ask: why did He say ﴿min fawqihinna﴾ (from above them)? I say: because the greatest signs and the most indicative of majesty and greatness are above the heavens: the Throne, the Footstool, and the ranks of angels who surround the Throne, glorifying and sanctifying, and what none knows the reality of except Allah, exalted is He, from the traces of His great dominion. Therefore He said ﴿yatafattarna min fawqihinna﴾, meaning, the splitting begins from their upper direction. Or: because the word of disbelief came from those beneath the heavens, so the analogy would be to say: "they split from beneath them, from the direction from which the word came." But this was exaggerated, so it was made to have effect in the direction of above, as if it were said: "they are about to split from the direction that is above them, leaving aside the direction that is beneath them." A parallel to this in exaggeration is His saying, mighty and high: ﴿Boiling water is poured over their heads﴾, ﴿by which what is in their bellies is melted﴾, where the boiling water is made to have effect on their inner parts. It was also said: ﴿from above them﴾ means from above the earths.

If you ask: how is it correct that they seek forgiveness for those on the earth, when among them are the disbelievers, the enemies of Allah? And Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Upon those is the curse of Allah and the angels﴾. How can they be cursing and seeking forgiveness for them? I say: His saying ﴿for those on the earth﴾ indicates the category of the people of the earth, and this categorical quality exists in all of them and in some of them, so it is permissible that this and that be intended. The proof has established that the angels do not seek forgiveness except for the friends of Allah, who are the believers, so Allah intended only them. Do you not see His saying in Surah al-Mu'min: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believed﴾, and His report about them: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾? How they described those for whom forgiveness is sought with what makes forgiveness deserved, and they did not leave, out of hope for their forgiveness, those among the believers who had not repented, so how would it be for the disbelievers? It is also possible that by seeking forgiveness they mean seeking forbearance and pardon, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing﴾. The intention is forbearance toward them and that He not hasten to punish them, so it is general.

If you ask: you have explained His saying ﴿the heavens are almost torn apart﴾ in two ways, so what is the correspondence of what follows to both of them? I say: as for one of them, it is as if it were said: "the heavens are about to split in awe of His majesty and in reverence for His greatness, and the angels, who fill the seven layers and surround the Throne in rows after rows, continue, in submission to His greatness, in worshipping, glorifying and praising Him, and they seek forgiveness for those on the earth out of fear for them from His might." As for the second, it is as if it were said: "they are about to split from the boldness of the people of polytheism in that monstrous word, while the angels declare Allah one and exalt Him above what is not permissible for Him of attributes which the ignorant ascribe to Him, praising Him for the kindnesses He has bestowed on them, by which He knows they are protected, choosing freely and not compelled, and they seek forgiveness for the believing people of the earth who have disassociated themselves from that word and from its speakers." Or they ask their Lord to show forbearance toward the people of the earth and not to hasten the punishment for them despite the presence of that among them, because of what they know of the benefits in that, and out of eagerness for the salvation of creation, and hope for the repentance of the disbelievers and the wicked among them.

Those who take protectors other than Him—God is watchful over them (ḥafīẓ ʿalayhim), a vigilant observer (raqīb) over their states and their deeds, nothing of which escapes Him; and He will call them to account for them and requite them. No one watches over them but Him alone. ﴿And you, O Muhammad, are not a guardian (mūkil) over them, nor have their affair entrusted to you, nor are you to compel them to faith.﴾ You are only a warner, nothing more.

Thus We revealed to you. This refers to the meaning of the verse before it: that God, exalted is He, is the Watcher over them, and you are not a watcher over them, but a warner to them, because God repeated this meaning in His Book in many places. The "kaf" (ka, "like this") is the object of awhayna (We revealed).

Qur'anan 'arabiyyan (an Arabic Qur'an) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object: We revealed it to you, and it is a clear Arabic Qur'an, with no ambiguity for you, so that you may understand what is said to you and not go beyond the limit of warning.

It is also permissible that "dhalika" (that) refers to the verbal noun (masdar) of awhayna: that is, "Such a clear, comprehensible revelation, We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an in your tongue, li-tundhira." One says anzartuhu kadha (I warned him of such-and-such) and anzartuhu bi-kadha (I warned him of such-and-such). The first, namely li-tundhira Umm al-Qura (to warn the Mother of Cities), has been transitive to both the first and second objects, and the second object is in His words, "and warn of the Day of Gathering" (tundhira yawm al-jam'); "Umm al-Qura" means the people of Umm al-Qura, as in His words, "And ask the town" (wa-as'al al-qarya), and "those around it" (wa man hawlaha) means the Arabs.

It is also recited as liyundhira (with the yā', so that He warns), the verb referring to the Qur'an. "Yawm al-jam'" (the Day of Gathering) is the Day of Resurrection, because the creatures will be gathered on it, as God, exalted is He, said: "The Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering" (Q. 64:9). It has been said that it means He gathers spirits and bodies together. It has also been said that it means He gathers every doer with his deed.

"La rayba fihi" (there is no doubt in it) is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) with no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu min al-i'rab).

It is recited: fariqun wa-fariqun (a group and a group), with raf' (nominative) and nasb (accusative). The nominative is read as: "Among them is a group, and among them is a group." The pronoun refers to those gathered, because the meaning is: the day the creatures are gathered.

The accusative is read as a circumstantial clause (hal) from them, that is, "scattered," as in His words: "And on the day the Hour is established, that day they will be divided" (Q. 30:14).

If you ask: how can they be gathered and scattered in one state? I answer: they are gathered on that day while being divided between the abodes of misery and bliss, just as people gather on Friday, scattered among two mosques. And if by gathering is meant their gathering at the place of standing, then scattering is in the sense of their being on the verge of separating.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 42, verse 8:**

﴿...He would have made them one community﴾, that is, all of them believers, by coercion and compulsion. This is like His saying ﴿And if We had willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾, and His saying ﴿And if your Lord had willed, all those on earth would have believed, all of them together﴾. The evidence that the meaning is compulsion into faith is His saying ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ and His saying ﴿Will you then compel...﴾, where the interrogative hamza (همزة الإنكار) is placed on the one being compelled (المكره، أي الذي يُكره) rather than on the verb (فعله) itself. This indicates that God alone is able to exercise this compulsion, and no other. The meaning is: if your Lord had willed a will of power (مشيئة قدرة), He would have compelled them all to believe. [[His saying "He would have compelled them all to believe" is the view of the Mu'tazila. As for Ahl al-Sunna, will (al-irada) entails the existence of what is willed, but it does not entail coercion or compulsion of the servants, since it does not contradict free choice (al-ikhtiyar), because they have acquisition (al-kasb) in their actions, even though these are created by God, exalted is He. As for the will that does not entail the willed object, which he calls the will of wisdom (مشيئة الحكمة), this is what the Mu'tazila take to mean command (الأمر), and Ahl al-Sunna do not affirm it, as established in the discussion of Tawhid (divine unity). Thus the meaning of the verse is: if your Lord had willed the faith of all, all would have believed, but He willed the faith of some, so whoever He willed to believe, believed. (ع)]] But He willed a will of wisdom (مشيئة حكمة), so He charged them and based their affair on what they choose, so that He might admit the believers into His mercy, and they are the ones meant by "whom He wills." Do you not see how He placed them in contrast with the wrongdoers, and leaves the wrongdoers without any protector or helper in His punishment?

The meaning of the interrogative hamza in "أَمِ الإنكار" (am al-inkar, the interrogative of denial): "فَاللَّهُ هُوَ الْوَلِيُّ" (So it is God who is the Protector) means: He is the one who must be taken as protector alone, and who must be believed to be the Lord and Master. The fa' in His words "فَاللَّهُ هُوَ الْوَلِيُّ" is the response to an implied condition, as if it were said, after denying every other protector: "If they seek a protector in truth, then God is the Protector in truth; there is no protector besides Him." "وَهُوَ يُحْيِ" (And He gives life) means: it is among the attributes of this Protector that "يُحْيِ الْمَوْتى" (He gives life to the dead). "وَهُوَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ" (And He is Powerful over everything) means: He is therefore the one deserving to be taken as protector, rather than those who have no power over anything.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 10:

"And whatever you differ about, its judgement is with Allah." This is a recounting of the words of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the believers. That is:

Whatever the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists opposed you in, so that you and they differed over it concerning some matter of the religion, the judgement regarding that matter of disagreement is entrusted to Allah, the Exalted: rewarding those among the believers who are right in it and punishing the wrongdoers. "That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied" in repelling the schemes of the enemies of the religion, "and to Him I turn" for sufficiency against their evil.

It has also been said: whatever you differed over and disputed concerning any of the disputes, then refer it for judgement to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and do not prefer any other's ruling over his ruling, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And if you dispute about anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger" (Qur'an 4:59).

It has also been said: whatever disagreement arose among you concerning the interpretation of a verse that was unclear to you, then return in its explanation to the clear (muhkam) verses of the Book of Allah and the apparent (zahir) content of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

And it has been said: whatever disagreement arose among you over the sciences that are not connected to your obligations and for which you have no path to knowledge, then say: "Allah knows best," such as knowledge of the soul (ruh). Allah, the Exalted, said: "They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is by the command of my Lord" (Qur'an 17:85).

If you say: Is it permissible to apply this to the disagreement of the mujtahids regarding the rulings of the Shari'ah? I say: No, because ijtihad (independent reasoning) is not permitted in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

**Fāṭir al-samāwāt** (the Originator of the heavens) is read in the nominative and in the genitive. The nominative makes it one of the predicates of *dhālikum* (that is your Lord). Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. The genitive reading means: "So His judgement is with God, the Originator of the heavens," and *dhālikum ilā* ("that is to") with *unību* ("I turn in repentance") is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tirāḍ*) placed between the adjective and the noun it modifies.

﴿*Jaʿala lakum min anfusikum azwājan*﴾ ("He made for you, from yourselves, mates"): *min anfusikum* means "from your own kind, from among humankind," and *azwājan* means "mates." ﴿*Wa min al-anʿāmi azwājan*﴾ ("and of the livestock, mates") means: He created, from the livestock, mates. The meaning is: He also created for the livestock, from their own kind, mates.

﴿*Yadhraukum*﴾ means "He multiplies you" (*yukaththirukum*). It is said: *dhara'a Allāh al-khalq*, meaning He scattered and multiplied the creatures. *Al-dharr*, *al-dharw* and *al-dharʾ* are cognates (*akhawāt*) of this root.

*Fīhi* ("in this") refers to this arrangement, namely that He made mates for humans and livestock, so that between their males and females there is procreation and reproduction. The pronoun in ﴿*yadhraukum*﴾ refers to the addressees and the livestock. The addressees, being rational beings, are given precedence (*taghlīb*) over the non-rational in the reference. The verse is one of those rulings that carry two grounds (*dhāt al-ʿillatayn*).

[[Mahmud said: "The pronoun attached to *yadhraʾu* refers to *al-anfus* and to the livestock, with the rational addressees given precedence over the non-rational in the reference, and this is one of the rulings that carry two grounds." Ahmad said: "The correct view is that these are two distinct rulings, not overlapping. The first is that the pronoun comes in the form of the rational plural, whether addressed or absent. The second is that after this it comes in the form of address. The first is for giving precedence to the rational (*taghlīb al-ʿaql*), and the second is for giving precedence to address (*taghlīb al-khiṭāb*)."]]

If you ask: what is the meaning of *yadhraukum fī hādhā al-tadbīr* ("He multiplies you in this arrangement"), and why was it not said *yadhraukum bihi* ("He multiplies you by it")? I answer: this arrangement is treated as the source and the mine (*al-manbaʿ wa al-maʿdin*) from which the scattering and multiplication come. Do you not say, of animals, that in the creation of pairs there is multiplication? As the Exalted said: ﴿*Wa lakum fī al-qiṣāṣi ḥayāh*﴾ ("And in retaliation there is life for you," Q. 2:179).

They say: "A man like you does not withhold" (*mithlu-ka lā yabkhal*). They negate stinginess from one like him, while they mean to negate it from himself. They intended emphasis by this, and so they took the path of allusion (*kināya*), because when they negate it from one who fills his place and who has his most distinctive attributes, they have negated it from him. Its parallel is your saying to an Arab: "The Arabs do not break covenants" (*al-ʿarab lā takhfar al-dhimam*). It is more eloquent than your saying "You do not break covenants."

[[His words "*lā takhfar al-dhimam* is more eloquent" — in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: *akhfartuhu* means I broke his covenant and betrayed him. And in it: "*ayfaʿa al-ghulām*" means the boy reached [the age of] adolescence (*ārtafaʿa*): he is *yāfiʿ*, and one does not say *mūfiʿ*. His words "*kāna ableegh*" perhaps have the implied sense: "If you say that to him, it would be more eloquent." (Ayn.)]] From your saying "You do not break covenants." From it is their saying: "He has come of age, and reached the age of his peers" (*qad ayfaʿat li-dāthihi wa balaghat atrābuhu*), meaning his coming of age and his reaching maturity.

In the hadith of Ruqayya bint Ṣayfī concerning the watering of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib: "Surely among them is the good and pure one, the peer of his contemporaries" (*al-ṭayyib al-ṭāhir li-dāthihi*), the intention is his purity and goodness. When it is known that this belongs to the category of allusion, there is no difference between your saying "There is nothing like God" (*laysa ka-Allāhi shayʾ*) and His saying ﴿*Laysa kamithlihi shayʾ*﴾ ("There is nothing like His likeness," Q. 42:11), except what allusion gives of its benefit. The two are like two expressions that alternate in one meaning: the negation of likeness from His essence.

Its parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿*Bal yadāhu mablūṭatān*﴾ ("Rather, both His hands are outspread," Q. 5:64). Its meaning is: rather, He is generous, without imagining a hand or an outspreading of it. This is because it has come to be an expression for generosity; they do not intend anything else by it. They even use it of one who has no hand. So likewise this is used of one who has a likeness and of one who has no likeness.

[[Mahmud said: "The Arabs say: 'A man like you does not withhold,' negating stinginess from his like, and what is meant is himself. Its parallel is your saying to an Arab: 'The Arabs do not break covenants.' And from it is their saying: 'He has come of age, and reached the age of his peers.' And in the hadith of Ruqayya bint Ṣayfī concerning the watering of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib: 'Surely among them is the good and pure one, the peer of his contemporaries,' meaning his purity and goodness. When it is known that this is from the category of allusion, there is no difference between your saying 'There is nothing like God' and His saying 'There is nothing like His likeness,' except what allusion gives of its benefit. Its parallel is His saying: 'Rather, both His hands are outspread,' for its meaning is: Rather, He is generous, without imagining a hand or spreading it, because it became an expression for generosity..." up to his words.

Ahmad said: "This second aspect is rejected, given what it contains of disturbing the meaning. What is fitting here is emphasis on the negation of likeness, while the *kāf* in this aspect only emphasizes likeness. There is a difference between emphasizing a negated likeness and emphasizing the negation of likeness. The negation of unqualified likeness is more eloquent and emphatic in meaning than the negation of likeness accompanied by emphasis, since the negation of unqualified likeness entails the negation of every likeness, whereas the negation of a firmly established and emphasized likeness does not entail the negation of a likeness lower than it in establishment and emphasis. Wherever the *kāf* comes emphasizing likeness, it comes in affirmation, and so it emphasizes it. Therefore the consideration of the verse by these two considerations is not sound, and God knows best. Among what guides to the soundness of what I have mentioned is that a speaker may say: 'Zayd is not like ʿAmr, but he is resembling him,' whereas if reversed it would not be correct. That is only because negating the lowest degree of resemblance entails negating its highest degree, but negating the highest degree does not entail negating the lowest. So when resemblance is emphasized, it falls short of the intensity. The first aspect he mentioned is the aspect of the verse in his view, and he brought the mount of weakness into this second aspect with his words 'And you may assert...' so understand."]]

Or you may hold that the word of comparison is repeated for emphasis, as in the saying of one who said:

*wa ṣāliyātin ka-kamā yu'thafīn*
("And hearths (of stones) blackened by fire, like the way they are set as tripods," Ruʾba-like, Lakhṭām al-Mujāshiʿī)

[[*Lam yabqa min āyin bihā yuḥlayn... ghayr ramādin wa ʿiẓāmin kuthafīn*
*wa ghayra wadd jādilin aw wadayn... wa ṣāliyātin ka-kamā yu'thafīn*
These are by Lakhṭām al-Mujāshiʿī. *Al-āy*: its singular is *āyah*, meaning sign. *Yuḥlayn*: a passive present from *ḥuliyyah*, from *ḥallaytuhu taḥliyatan*, when his attribute is described, that is, his qualities are described. He says: there remained of the traces of these abodes no signs in them describing their qualities, except ashes and bones piled up and heaped. *Al-kashf* (with a vowel on the first letter) is like *sabab*, meaning the gathering, and he perhaps vowelled it for the metre. It is also transmitted as: "*ghayr ramādin wa khiṭāmin kuthafīn*." *Al-khiṭām* is the halter; it is also transmitted with the unpointed letter, meaning what is broken and snapped of dry firewood. *Al-kathf* (as *ḥiml*) is the vessel for pasturing, so *kuthafīn* is with the conjunction omitted. It is also said to be a substitute for what precedes it. The better transmission is *wa khiṭāma kuthafīn* with the genitive construction, for the sake of agreement with the rhyme, meaning: and the halter of two vessels. He repeated the particle of exception for emphasis. *Al-wadd* is originally a stake; the *tāʾ* was changed to *dāl* and assimilated into the other one among Tamim, as an anomaly. *Al-jādil* is the erect and thick, meaning: there remained only one stake standing there, or two stakes and nothing else, since he did not doubt except in that. *Al-ṣāliyāt* is an attribute of the tripods. It is also said to be an attribute of the women who kindle the fire, and it is also said to be an attribute of the horses that are hardened for war, like the tripods hardened for fire, but these two do not suit the description of the abode as empty. *Al-uthfiyyah* is the stone of the hearth; its form is originally *uftu'ulah*, and its plural is *athāfī*. *Uthfiyat li-l-qidr* means I placed the tripods for the cooking pot, and *thaffaytuhā tathfiyatan* means I set it on the tripods. His words *yu'thafīn* are a passive present, coming in the original form with hamza, like *yu'kar* from *bi-l-hamza*. This indicates that *ṣāliyāt* is an attribute of the stones that are constantly by the fire and burnt by it. Perhaps he likened the women to the tripods for their ugliness and blackness, through the abundance of smoke and their constant presence at the fire.

On this basis the meaning is: "and women hardened by fire like stones set to be placed under the cooking pot." So *mā* is a relative pronoun referring to the stones, not a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) or restrictive (*kāffah*) particle. The *kāf* of comparison is repeated for emphasis, but the second is a noun meaning "like," because the preposition does not enter upon its like. It is possible that he repeated the particle without repeating the genitive noun, as an anomaly.

It is transmitted after his words "*wa ṣāliyāt...*" etc.:

*lā yashtakayna ʿamalan mā anqayn... mā dāma mukhkhun fī salāmā aw ʿayn*
("They do not complain of toil so long as they are fattened... so long as marrow is in their phalanges or eye.") This suits the statement that they are an attribute of the mares or women, in the earlier comparison. *Al-inqāʾ* is the abundance of *al-naqy*, which is marrow. It is said: "*anqat al-ibil*" when the camels grew fat and their marrow increased, meaning: they do not complain of work during the period of their fattening and fleshiness, and he explained that by his words "so long as marrow..." *Al-salāmiyyāt* are the bones of the fingers, and they and the eye are the last parts in which the marrow remains.

It is also transmitted thus:

*ahal ʿarafat al-dār bi-l-Ghuraynī... wa ṣāliyāt ka-kamā yu'thafīn*
*Al-Ghuraynān* are two tall structures; it is said they are the graves of Mālik and ʿAqīl, the boon-companions of Judhayma al-Abrash. They were so called because al-Nuʿmān used to make them drink wine on the day of his misfortune when he went out to kill them. The more likely view is that this is a confusion by the transmitter, and that *ṣāliyāt* means the stones. His words "*lā yashtakayna...*" etc. are not from this rajaz, so it should not be transmitted with it. It is the one describing mares, or the women of origin rather than the *ṣāliyāt*. It is possible that the rajaz is thus:

*ahal ʿarafat al-dār bi-l-Ghuraynī... lam yabqa min āyin bihā yuḥlayn*
and that his words "*lā yashtakayna...*" are from another place in that rajaz, describing the horses, as the author of *al-Kāfī* transmitted it as evidence for rhyming with different consonants (*al-akfāʾ fī al-qāfiyah*) thus:

*banāt waṭāʾ ʿalā khadd al-layl... lā yashtakayna ʿamalan mā anqayn*
because the two rhyme letters differ. *Al-waṭṭāʾ* (with damma and shadda) is from treading upon the ground. *Khadd al-layl* is its path which is only travelled in it. Some say: this is in the description of horses, and that it is from the *mashṭūr* of *al-munsarih al-mawqūf*. And according to the view that it is in the description of a camel (*ajal*), it means: so the mounts are daughters of she-camels or stallions, *waṭṭāʾ* being the plural of *wāṭiʾ* or *wāṭiʾah*, treading upon the cheek of the night. This is a metaphor for their strength in travelling, such that they seem to overcome the night, so it is left behind and they tread upon its cheek, and they do not care about it.]]

Or as the saying of one who said:

*fa-aṣbaḥat mithla kaʿaṣfin maʾkūl*
("Yesterday they were in prosperity, hoped for... and they became like chaff eaten.")

[[*Bi-l-amsi kānat fī rakhāʾin maʾmūl... fa-aṣbaḥat mithla kaʿaṣfin maʾkūl*
It is transmitted, attributed to Ruʾba, with this substitution:
*wa laʿibat ṭayru bihim abābīl... fa-ṣayyarū mithla kaʿaṣfin maʾkūl*
He says: *bi-l-amsi*, meaning in the recent past, those abodes were a proverb for prosperity, that is, fertility and abundance of wealth and riches, hoped for by people, meaning desired by people. He repeated the word of comparison for emphasis. *Al-ʿaṣf* is what is on the grain and on the stalk of the crop of the dry figs and leaves. *Maʾkūl* means struck by the blight, and this is the worm. Beasts have eaten it and then voided it. *Abābīl* means scattered groups; it is an attribute of birds, and it is a plural noun with no singular from its own form. It is said: its singular is *abūl*, like *ʿujūl*. It is said: *ibāl*, like *miftāḥ*. It is said: *ibīl*, like *miskīn*. As for Ruʾba's *ṣayyarū*, it is with the shadda and the passive form, and perhaps this rajaz is another one.]]
Also recited: "wa-yaqdiru" (and He measures out). ﴿Indeed He is Knowing of all things.﴾ So when He knows that wealth is good for the servant, He enriches him; otherwise, He impoverishes him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 13:

He prescribed for you of the religion that which He enjoined upon Nuh (Noah), and that which We revealed to you (O Muhammad ﷺ), and that which We enjoined upon Ibrahim, Musa and Isa, and those prophets who came between them. Then he explained the thing prescribed, in which these great messengers all share, with His words ﴿that you establish the religion and do not divide over it﴾. What is meant is the establishment of the religion of Islam, which is the affirmation of God's oneness and obedience to Him, belief in His messengers and His books, in the Day of Recompense, and all that by establishing which a person becomes a Muslim. It does not mean the sharia (sharia, the sacred law) which are the welfare arrangements of nations according to their circumstances, for these differ and vary. God the Exalted said: ﴿To each of you We have appointed a law (shir'a, a way) and a method (minhaj, a clear path)﴾.

The place of ﴿an-aqimu (that you establish)﴾ is either in the accusative as a substitute (badal, apposition) for the object of "shara'a" and what is coordinated with it, or in the nominative as a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were said: "What is that which was prescribed?" So it was said: "It is the establishing of the religion." Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾.

﴿Grievous to the polytheists﴾: it was great and burdensome upon them, ﴿that to which you call them﴾, namely the establishment of God's religion and monotheism. ﴿God chooses for Himself﴾: He draws to it and gathers [to it]. The pronoun refers to the religion, through success and guidance. ﴿Whomever He wills﴾: whom His success benefits among them, and upon whom His grace flows.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 14:

And they did not become divided, meaning the People of the Book after their prophets, except after knowledge had come to them, namely that division is misguidance and corruption, and a matter for which a threat has been issued through the tongues of the prophets. ﴿And had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord﴾, which is the decree of delay until the Day of Resurrection, ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾ at the time they divided, because of the enormity of what they committed. ﴿And indeed those who were given the Book after them﴾, who are the People of the Book who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿are in grave doubt concerning it, not believing in it with true belief﴾. It is said: mankind was one community of believers after Allah had destroyed all the people of the earth by the Flood. When the fathers died, the sons differed among themselves, and that was when Allah sent to them the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and knowledge came to them. They differed only out of rebellion among themselves. It is also said: the People of the Book did not become divided except after knowledge of the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had come to them, like His saying, ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof had come to them﴾. And as for ﴿those who were given the Book after them﴾, they are the polytheists: they were given the Qur'an after the People of the Book had been given the Torah and the Gospel.

It was also read: wa-warrithū and wa-waratha (with the verb read in two forms of transmission, one with the doubled ra' and one without).

Therefore (fa-li-dhalika), that is, because of the division and what resulted from it, namely the splintering of disbelief into sects, call (to unity and harmony upon the ancient upright religion), and be steadfast (upon it and upon calling to it, as God has commanded you), and do not follow their (divergent, false) desires, (by) whatever Book God has sent down, of whatever Book it is established that God sent down, meaning belief in all the revealed Books, because those who divided believed in some and disbelieved in others, like His saying, ﴿And they say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others,"﴾ up to His saying, ﴿Those are the disbelievers in truth.﴾ ﴿God has commanded me to act justly between you﴾ in judgment, when you dispute and come to me for judgment. ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, meaning there is no dispute, because the truth has become manifest and you have been overcome by it, so there is no need for argument. Its meaning is: there is no presenting of proofs between us, because disputants each present their own proof, and this one presents his proof and that one presents his proof. ﴿God will gather us together on the Day of Resurrection, and to Him is the final return﴾; He will judge between us and take vengeance for us upon you. This is a disengagement and a parting of ways after the truth has become manifest and the proof and obligation have been established. If you say: how can they be disengaged from, when after that there was done to them what was done, of killing, destruction of homes, cutting down of palm trees, and expulsion? I say: what is meant is disengagement from them in the situations of verbal debate, not of fighting.

Those who argue about God (يُحَاجُّونَ فِي اللَّهِ), disputing about His religion (يخاصمون في دينه), after it has been responded to (مِنْ بَعْدِ ما استجاب له الناس) and people have entered into Islam (ودخلوا في الإسلام), in order to turn them back to the religion of ignorance (ليردّوهم إلى دين الجاهلية). Like the saying of the Exalted (كقوله تعالى): ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your belief﴾. The Jews and Christians used to say to the believers: "Our Book is before your Book, and our Prophet is before your Prophet, and we are better than you [[The phrase "and we are better than you" is perhaps originally "so we are", like the wording of al-Nasafi. (Editor's note)]] and more deserving of the truth." It was also said: "after God responded to His Messenger and granted him victory on the day of Badr and made the religion of Islam manifest." ﴿Their argument is futile (داحِضَةٌ)﴾, meaning false and slipping away (زالة).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 17–18:

﴿Allah is He who has sent down the Book (al-Kitab) with the truth, and the Balance (al-Mizan).﴾ That is, the genus of the Book (al-kitab) and the Balance (al-mizan), which is justice (al-adl) and equity (al-taswiyah). The meaning of "sending down justice" is that He sent it down in His revealed books. It has also been said: the Balance is that by which things are weighed.

"With the truth": accompanied by the truth, joined to it, far from falsehood, or with the correct purpose as wisdom requires; or with what is obligatory of permitting and forbidding and other things.

﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ The Hour refers to the interpretation of the Resurrection (al-ba'th), and therefore it is said, "near"; or the meaning is that the coming of the Hour is near.

If you say: how does the mention of the nearness of the Hour fit with the sending down of the Book and the Balance? I say: because the Hour is the Day of Reckoning and the setting up of the scales for justice, so it is as if it were said: Allah has commanded you to justice, equity, and acting upon the laws before the Day arrives suddenly, the Day on which He will call you to account and weigh your deeds, and give full measure to whoever gave full measure and cheat whoever cheated.

Al-Mira' (disputation): al-mulajjah [[His saying "al-mulajjah" with a jim: persistence in dispute; yumrii means: he extracts, as stated in al-Sihah. (ع)]], because each of the two disputants extracts what is in the other's possession.

﴿Those who dispute about the Hour are in far-off error.﴾ That is, far from the truth.

Because the establishment of the Hour is not remote from the power of Allah, and because the inimitable Book indicates that it is coming, there is no doubt in it, and because the intellects testify that there must be an abode of recompense.

Allah is Latif (Gentle, Subtly Kind) to His servants: Kind in the fullest sense of kindness toward them. His kindness reaches all of them, and from each of them it reaches to where no one else can attain. They are one of His universals and particulars.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, "He provides for whom He wills," after His kindness has reached all of them? I say: all of them are recipients of kindness, and none is free of His kindness. However, kindness is of various kinds and has various attributes. The distribution among the servants varies according to the variations of the matters of wisdom and management. So one kind of kindness alights upon some servants that did not alight upon another, and this one receives a share with an attribute that is not the attribute of his companion's share. Thus whoever is allotted from them what is not allotted to the other has been provided for, and this is what He intends by His saying, "He provides for whom He wills," just as one of two brothers is given a child while the other is not, though the one who was not given a child is favoured with another blessing. "And He is the Strong (al-Qawiyy), the One of overpowering capacity, Dominant over everything; the Mighty (al-'Aziz), the Invincible who cannot be overcome."

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 20:

He called what the worker does, by which he seeks benefit and growth (al-zakāʾ), "tilth" (ḥarth) by way of metaphor (majāz). And he distinguished between the two deeds of the two kinds of workers:

For whoever works for the Hereafter, his work is made successful and his good deeds are multiplied. Whoever's work is for this world, he is given some of it, but not what he desires and seeks. That is his provision which has been apportioned for him and is finished, and he has no share at all in the Hereafter. He did not say, in the sense of the worker for the Hereafter, that he also has a share in this world, on the basis that his apportioned provision reaches him without fail, belittling that in comparison with what he is aiming at, namely the growth of his work and his success in the place of return.

The meaning of the hamza in "am" is for confirmation and rebuke. "Their partners" (shurakā'uhum): their devils, who adorned for them polytheism, denial of the resurrection, and working for the world, since they know nothing other than it; this is the religion which the devils prescribed for them, and God is exalted above permitting it or commanding it. It was also said that "their partners" are their idols. They are attributed to them because they took them as partners with God, so at times they are ascribed to them on account of this association, and at times to God. And since they were the cause of their misguidance and seduction, they were made to legislate for the religion of disbelief, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, they have led many of mankind astray﴾. And ﴿Were it not for a word of decision﴾, that is, the prior decree to postpone the recompense; that is, were it not for the promise that the decision would take place on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿it would have been judged between them﴾, that is, between the disbelievers and the believers, or between the polytheists and their partners. Muslim ibn Jundab read "wa-anna al-ẓālimīna" with a fatḥa, as a conjunction upon "kalimat al-faṣl" (the word of decision), meaning: were it not for the word of decision and the determination of the punishment of the wrongdoers in the Hereafter, it would have been judged between them in this world.

﴿تَرَى الظَّالِمِينَ فِي الْآخِرَةِ مُشْفِقِينَ مِمَّا كَسَبُوا وَهُوَ وَاقِعٌ بِهِمْ﴾ ("You will see the wrongdoers fearful of what they have earned, and it will befall them.") Meaning: they will be in a state of extreme fear and their hearts will be tormented by what they have earned of evil deeds. "And it will befall them" means its consequence (wabāl) will reach them and will inevitably attach to them, whether they feel fear or not.

﴿فِي رَوْضَةِ الْجَنَّةِ﴾ ("in the meadows of Paradise"). The meadow of the believer's Paradise is the most pleasant and most delightful spot in it. ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("with their Lord") is in the accusative, governed by the adverb of place, and is connected to ﴿يَشَاءُونَ﴾ ("they will have whatever they wish").

It was read as ﴿يُبَشِّرُ﴾ ("He gives good news of"), from bashshara; and as ﴿يُبْشِرُ﴾, from abshara; and as ﴿يَبْشُرُ﴾, from bashara. The underlying sense is: "That is the reward with which God gives good news to His servants," where the preposition has been elided, as in the verse ﴿وَاخْتَارَ مُوسَى قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("Moses chose his people"), and then the returning pronoun to the relative has been elided, as in the verse ﴿أَهَذَا الَّذِي بَعَثَ اللَّهُ رَسُولًا﴾ ("Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?"). Or it means: "That is the good news which God gives to His servants."

It is related that the polytheists gathered in one of their assemblies, and some of them said to others: "Do you think Muhammad asks for a reward for what he undertakes?" Then the verse was revealed:

﴿قُل لَّا أَسْأَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ أَجْرًا إِلَّا الْمَوَدَّةَ فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ﴾ ("Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin.")

The exception may be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: "I do not ask you for any reward except this, that you love my kinsfolk." This was not truly a reward, because his kinship was their kinship, so maintaining ties with them was binding upon them as a matter of honour. It may also be a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "I do not ask you for any reward at all, but I do ask you to love my kinsfolk, who are your kinsfolk, and not to harm them."

If you ask: Why was it not said "except the love of kinship" (إلا مودة القربى), or "except the love for the kinship" (إلا المودة للقربى)? And what is the meaning of ﴿إِلَّا الْمَوَدَّةَ فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ﴾? I answer: they made the kinsfolk a place for love and a dwelling for it, as when you say: "I have love (mawaddah) for the family of so-and-so," and "I have a strong passion and intense love for them," meaning: "I love them, and they are the place of my love and its locus." The preposition (fi) here is not connected to the noun "love" as the lam would be in "except the love for the kinship." It is connected to an elided verb, in the way that a adverb of place is connected to its verb in your saying: "The money is in the bag." Its implied sense is: "except that love is firmly established within the kinship and settled in it."

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask, why was it not said: 'except the love of kinship,' or 'except the love for the kinship'? He answered: they made a place for love and a dwelling for it, as when you say: 'I have passion and intense love for the family of so-and-so,' and it is not in a complement to the love, as the lam would be if you said 'except the love for the kinship.' It is connected to an elided element whose implied sense is: 'except that love is established in the kinship and settled in it.'" Ahmad said: This is the meaning that was intended by his statement, in the verse mentioned earlier, that His saying ﴿يَذْرَؤُكُمْ فِيهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you through it") came as a substitute for His saying ﴿يَذْرَؤُكُمْ بِهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you by it"). So understand it.]]

The word "al-qurba" (القربى) is a verbal noun like "al-zulfa" and "al-busra," meaning "kinship." What is meant is the people of kinship.

It is related that when this verse was revealed, it was said: "O Messenger of God, who are these kinsmen of yours whose love has become obligatory upon us?" He said: "ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, and their two sons."

[[Recorded by al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim in (the book on) the virtues of al-Shafi'i, from the narration of Husayn al-Ashqar, from Qays ibn al-Rabi', from al-A'mash, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Husayn is weak and discarded. And what is stronger than him has contradicted him. In al-Bukhari, from the narration of Tawus, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he was asked about this verse. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The kinsfolk of the family of Muhammad ﷺ?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "You have been hasty. The Prophet ﷺ had no clan of Quraysh except that he had kinship with them" — the hadith. I say: Sa'id ibn Mansur also recorded from the path of al-Sha'bi, who said: "They made many (claims) about us concerning this verse, so we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he wrote" — he mentioned something similar, and Ibn Tawus's (report) is more complete than it.]]

This is supported by what is related from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "I complained to the Messenger of God ﷺ about the envy of people toward me. He said: 'Are you not content to be the fourth of four? The first to enter Paradise are I, you, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, with our wives on our right and left, and our offspring behind our wives.'"

[[Recorded by al-Karimi from Ibn ʿAʾishah with his chain from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him. And al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Abu Rafiʿ, that the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAlī: "The first four who will enter Paradise are—" and he mentioned it. Its chain is weak.]]

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Paradise is forbidden to whoever wrongs my household and harms me regarding my kindred. And whoever does a favour to someone from the children of ʿAbd al-Muttalib and he does not repay it, I will repay it for him tomorrow, when he meets me on the Day of Resurrection."

[[Recorded by al-Tha'labi from the hadith of ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him. In it is ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn ʿAmir al-Ta'i from his father, and he is a liar.]]

It is also related that the Ansar said: "We did this and we did that," as if they were boasting. Then al-ʿAbbās, or Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "We have the superiority over you." This reached the Messenger of God ﷺ, so he came to them in their assemblies and said: "O assembly of the Ansar, were you not humble, and did God not strengthen you through me?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Were you not astray, and did God not guide you through me?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Will you not answer me?"

[[Recorded by al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, all from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas. In it is Yazid ibn Ziyad, who is weak.]]

They said: "What should we say, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Will you not say: 'Did your people not drive you out, and we gave you refuge? Or did they not deny you, and we believed you? Or did they not forsake you, and we helped you?'" He kept on saying this until they fell upon their knees and said: "Our wealth and what is in our hands belongs to God and His Messenger." Then the verse was revealed.

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies as a martyr.

[[Recorded by al-Tha'labi: "Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Balkhi informed us, Yaʿqub ibn Yusuf ibn Ishaq informed us, Muhammad ibn Aslam informed us, Yaʿla ibn ʿUbayd informed us, from Isma'il ibn Qays, from Jarir" — at length. Signs of fabrication are evident in it. Muhammad and those above him are trustworthy. The defect in it lies between al-Tha'labi and Muhammad.]]

Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies forgiven. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies repentant. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies a believer with perfect faith. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad, the Angel of Death gives him the good news of Paradise, then Munkar and Nakir. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad is escorted to Paradise as a bride is escorted to her husband's house. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad, two doors to Paradise are opened for him in his grave. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad, God makes his grave a place visited by the angels of mercy. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies upon the Sunnah and the Jama'ah. Beware: whoever dies upon hatred for the family of Muhammad comes on the Day of Resurrection with "written between his eyes" [[The phrase "maktub bayna ʿaynayhi" (written between his eyes) is perhaps "maktuban" (in the accusative). (ʿ)]]: "Despairing of the mercy of God." Beware: whoever dies upon hatred for the family of Muhammad dies a disbeliever. Beware: whoever dies upon hatred for the family of Muhammad will not smell the fragrance of Paradise."

It was also said: There was no clan of the clans of Quraysh except that there was kinship between the Messenger of God ﷺ and them. When they denied him and refused to pledge allegiance to him, this verse was revealed. The meaning is: "except that you love me for the sake of kinship," that is, for its right and on its account, as you say: "love for God's sake and hatred for God's sake," meaning: for His right and on His account. The sense is: "You are my people and the most deserving of those who should respond to me and obey me. Since you have refused that, then preserve the right of kinship, do not harm me, and do not incite against me."

It was also said: The Ansar came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with wealth they had gathered and said: "O Messenger of God, God has guided us through you, you are the son of our sister, calamities and obligations befall you, and your wealth is limited, so seek help with this for what befalls you." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi in (their books on) the occasions of revelation, from Ibn ʿAbbas, without a chain. It is likely from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from him. Al-Tabarani recorded it through ʿUthman ibn al-Qattan, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him. Then the verse was revealed and he rejected it.

It was also said: "al-qurba" means seeking nearness to God, meaning: "except that you love God and His Messenger through your seeking nearness to Him by obedience and righteous deeds."

It is read as ﴿إِلَّا مَوَدَّةً فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ﴾ ("except love in kinship").

﴿وَمَن يَقْتَرِفْ حَسَنَةً نَّزِدْ لَهُ فِيهَا حُسْنًا﴾ ("And whoever earns a good deed, We increase for him good in it"). It is related from al-Suddi that it refers to love for the family of the Messenger of God ﷺ; it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, and his love for them. The apparent meaning is generality: whatever good deed it is. However, since it was mentioned after the mention of love in kinship, that indicates that it primarily refers to love, as if all other good deeds were its followers.

It is read as ﴿نَزِدْ﴾ ("We increase"), meaning God increases. The increase of its goodness from God's side is its multiplication, as in His saying: ﴿مَن ذَا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا فَيُضَاعِفَهُ لَهُ أَضْعَافًا كَثِيرَةً﴾ ("Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so He will multiply it for him manifold").

It is also read as ﴿حُسْنَىٰ﴾ ("the best"), which is a verbal noun like "al-busra" (good news).

﴿الشَّكُورُ﴾ ("the Most Appreciative") is, in the description of God, a metaphor for taking account of obedience, fulfilling its reward, and bestowing favour upon the one who is rewarded.

It is related that the polytheists gathered in one of their assemblies, and some of them said to others: "Do you think Muhammad asks for a reward for what he undertakes?" Then the verse was revealed:

﴿قُل لَّا أَسْأَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ أَجْرًا إِلَّا الْمَوَدَّةَ فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ﴾ ("Say: I do not ask you any reward for it, except love for the near of kin.")

The exception may be a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), meaning: "I do not ask you for any reward except this, that you love my kinsfolk." This was not truly a reward, because his kinship was their kinship, so maintaining ties with them was binding upon them as a matter of honour. It may also be a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: "I do not ask you for any reward at all, but I do ask you to love my kinsfolk, who are your kinsfolk, and not to harm them."

If you ask: Why was it not said "except the love of kinship" (إلا مودة القربى), or "except the love for the kinship" (إلا المودة للقربى)? And what is the meaning of ﴿إِلَّا الْمَوَدَّةَ فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ﴾? I answer: they made the kinsfolk a place for love and a dwelling for it, as when you say: "I have love (mawaddah) for the family of so-and-so," and "I have a strong passion and intense love for them," meaning: "I love them, and they are the place of my love and its locus." The preposition (fi) here is not connected to the noun "love" as the lam would be in "except the love for the kinship." It is connected to an elided verb, in the way that a adverb of place is connected to its verb in your saying: "The money is in the bag." Its implied sense is: "except that love is firmly established within the kinship and settled in it."

[[Mahmud said: "If you ask, why was it not said: 'except the love of kinship,' or 'except the love for the kinship'? He answered: they made a place for love and a dwelling for it, as when you say: 'I have passion and intense love for the family of so-and-so,' and it is not in a complement to the love, as the lam would be if you said 'except the love for the kinship.' It is connected to an elided element whose implied sense is: 'except that love is established in the kinship and settled in it.'" Ahmad said: This is the meaning that was intended by his statement, in the verse mentioned earlier, that His saying ﴿يَذْرَؤُكُمْ فِيهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you through it") came as a substitute for His saying ﴿يَذْرَؤُكُمْ بِهِ﴾ ("He multiplies you by it"). So understand it.]]

The word "al-qurba" (القربى) is a verbal noun like "al-zulfa" and "al-busra," meaning "kinship." What is meant is the people of kinship.

It is related that when this verse was revealed, it was said: "O Messenger of God, who are these kinsmen of yours whose love has become obligatory upon us?" He said: "ʿAlī, Fāṭimah, and their two sons."

[[Recorded by al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim in (the book on) the virtues of al-Shafi'i, from the narration of Husayn al-Ashqar, from Qays ibn al-Rabi', from al-A'mash, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Husayn is weak and discarded. And what is stronger than him has contradicted him. In al-Bukhari, from the narration of Tawus, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he was asked about this verse. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "The kinsfolk of the family of Muhammad ﷺ?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "You have been hasty. The Prophet ﷺ had no clan of Quraysh except that he had kinship with them" — the hadith. I say: Sa'id ibn Mansur also recorded from the path of al-Sha'bi, who said: "They made many (claims) about us concerning this verse, so we wrote to Ibn ʿAbbas, and he wrote" — he mentioned something similar, and Ibn Tawus's (report) is more complete than it.]]

This is supported by what is related from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "I complained to the Messenger of God ﷺ about the envy of people toward me. He said: 'Are you not content to be the fourth of four? The first to enter Paradise are I, you, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, with our wives on our right and left, and our offspring behind our wives.'"

[[Recorded by al-Karimi from Ibn ʿAʾishah with his chain from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him. And al-Tabarani narrated it from the hadith of Abu Rafiʿ, that the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAlī: "The first four who will enter Paradise are—" and he mentioned it. Its chain is weak.]]

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Paradise is forbidden to whoever wrongs my household and harms me regarding my kindred. And whoever does a favour to someone from the children of ʿAbd al-Muttalib and he does not repay it, I will repay it for him tomorrow, when he meets me on the Day of Resurrection."

[[Recorded by al-Tha'labi from the hadith of ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him. In it is ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn ʿAmir al-Ta'i from his father, and he is a liar.]]

It is also related that the Ansar said: "We did this and we did that," as if they were boasting. Then al-ʿAbbās, or Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "We have the superiority over you." This reached the Messenger of God ﷺ, so he came to them in their assemblies and said: "O assembly of the Ansar, were you not humble, and did God not strengthen you through me?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Were you not astray, and did God not guide you through me?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Will you not answer me?"

[[Recorded by al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, all from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas. In it is Yazid ibn Ziyad, who is weak.]]

They said: "What should we say, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Will you not say: 'Did your people not drive you out, and we gave you refuge? Or did they not deny you, and we believed you? Or did they not forsake you, and we helped you?'" He kept on saying this until they fell upon their knees and said: "Our wealth and what is in our hands belongs to God and His Messenger." Then the verse was revealed.

The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies as a martyr.

[[Recorded by al-Tha'labi: "Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli al-Balkhi informed us, Yaʿqub ibn Yusuf ibn Ishaq informed us, Muhammad ibn Aslam informed us, Yaʿla ibn ʿUbayd informed us, from Isma'il ibn Qays, from Jarir" — at length. Signs of fabrication are evident in it. Muhammad and those above him are trustworthy. The defect in it lies between al-Tha'labi and Muhammad.]]

Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies forgiven. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies repentant. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies a believer with perfect faith. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad, the Angel of Death gives him the good news of Paradise, then Munkar and Nakir. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad is escorted to Paradise as a bride is escorted to her husband's house. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad, two doors to Paradise are opened for him in his grave. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad, God makes his grave a place visited by the angels of mercy. Beware: whoever dies upon love for the family of Muhammad dies upon the Sunnah and the Jama'ah. Beware: whoever dies upon hatred for the family of Muhammad comes on the Day of Resurrection with "written between his eyes" [[The phrase "maktub bayna ʿaynayhi" (written between his eyes) is perhaps "maktuban" (in the accusative). (ʿ)]]: "Despairing of the mercy of God." Beware: whoever dies upon hatred for the family of Muhammad dies a disbeliever. Beware: whoever dies upon hatred for the family of Muhammad will not smell the fragrance of Paradise."

It was also said: There was no clan of the clans of Quraysh except that there was kinship between the Messenger of God ﷺ and them. When they denied him and refused to pledge allegiance to him, this verse was revealed. The meaning is: "except that you love me for the sake of kinship," that is, for its right and on its account, as you say: "love for God's sake and hatred for God's sake," meaning: for His right and on His account. The sense is: "You are my people and the most deserving of those who should respond to me and obey me. Since you have refused that, then preserve the right of kinship, do not harm me, and do not incite against me."

It was also said: The Ansar came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with wealth they had gathered and said: "O Messenger of God, God has guided us through you, you are the son of our sister, calamities and obligations befall you, and your wealth is limited, so seek help with this for what befalls you." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi in (their books on) the occasions of revelation, from Ibn ʿAbbas, without a chain. It is likely from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from him. Al-Tabarani recorded it through ʿUthman ibn al-Qattan, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas. Ibn Mardawayh also recorded it from him. Then the verse was revealed and he rejected it.

It was also said: "al-qurba" means seeking nearness to God, meaning: "except that you love God and His Messenger through your seeking nearness to Him by obedience and righteous deeds."

It is read as ﴿إِلَّا مَوَدَّةً فِي الْقُرْبَىٰ﴾ ("except love in kinship").

﴿وَمَن يَقْتَرِفْ حَسَنَةً نَّزِدْ لَهُ فِيهَا حُسْنًا﴾ ("And whoever earns a good deed, We increase for him good in it"). It is related from al-Suddi that it refers to love for the family of the Messenger of God ﷺ; it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, and his love for them. The apparent meaning is generality: whatever good deed it is. However, since it was mentioned after the mention of love in kinship, that indicates that it primarily refers to love, as if all other good deeds were its followers.

It is read as ﴿نَزِدْ﴾ ("We increase"), meaning God increases. The increase of its goodness from God's side is its multiplication, as in His saying: ﴿مَن ذَا الَّذِي يُقْرِضُ اللَّهَ قَرْضًا حَسَنًا فَيُضَاعِفَهُ لَهُ أَضْعَافًا كَثِيرَةً﴾ ("Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so He will multiply it for him manifold").

It is also read as ﴿حُسْنَىٰ﴾ ("the best"), which is a verbal noun like "al-busra" (good news).

﴿الشَّكُورُ﴾ ("the Most Appreciative") is, in the description of God, a metaphor for taking account of obedience, fulfilling its reward, and bestowing favour upon the one who is rewarded.

Am (the particle "am," here used as munqati'a, "disconnected") — and the hamza in it carries the sense of reproach (tawbikh). It is as if it were said: "Which of the two is it? Do they think it likely that he would ascribe to God something like this [lies], and then, beyond that, the fabrication against God, which is the greatest and most abominable of fabrications? ﴿If God willed, He would seal up your heart﴾, meaning: if God willed, He would make you one of those whose hearts are sealed, so that you would fabricate lies against Him, for only one who is in the same condition as they would dare to fabricate lies against God." This manner of speech conveys that fabrication from someone like him is far-fetched, and that it is as remote as associating partners with God and entering into the category of those whose hearts are sealed. An example of this: a man who wishes to accuse a trustworthy person of betrayal, but says, "Perhaps God has forsaken me, perhaps God has blinded my heart," while he does not actually mean to affirm forsaking or blindness of heart. He only means to express the remoteness of accusing such a person, and to draw attention to the great matter in which he has involved himself by making that accusation.

Then he said: "It is God's custom to erase falsehood and establish truth by His words, by His revelation or His decree," as in His saying, ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it﴾. The meaning: if he were a fabricator as you claim, God would have exposed his fabrication, destroyed him, and hurled the truth against his falsehood so that it crushed it. It is also permissible that this be a promise to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that He will erase the falsehood in which they stand, namely slander (buhtan) and denial, and establish the truth you are upon through the Qur'an and through His decree, which cannot be turned back, of granting you victory over them. ﴿Indeed God knows what is in your breast and their breasts﴾, so the matter proceeds in accordance with that.

It is reported from Qatadah concerning ﴿He would seal up your heart﴾: He would make you forget the Qur'an and cut off revelation from you, meaning: if he had fabricated lies against God, this is what would have been done to him. It has also been said that ﴿He would seal up your heart﴾ means He would bind his heart with patience, so that their harm would not burden you.

If you say: "If His saying ﴿And God erases falsehood﴾ is an independent sentence not conjoined to 'He would seal,' then why is the waw (and) omitted in the script?" I say: it is omitted just as it is omitted in His saying ﴿Man prays for evil﴾ and His saying ﴿We shall call the guards of Hell﴾, although it is written in some of the copies of the Qur'an.

It is said: "I accepted the thing from him" (قبلت منه الشيء) and "I accepted it from him" (قبلته عنه). The meaning of *qabiltuhu minhu* is: I took it from him and made it the starting point and origin of my acceptance. The meaning of *qabiltuhu 'anhu* is: I separated myself from it and distanced myself from it.

*Tawbah* (repentance, the turning back to God from sin) is turning away from wrongdoing and from neglecting an obligation, through regret over both and the resolve never to return to them, because what one turns away from is wrongdoing and the neglect of an obligation. If the sin involved the right of a servant, then there is no escape except by way of restitution.

Jabir narrated that a Bedouin entered the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance," and he said the takbir. When he finished his prayer, Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "O man, quickness of the tongue in seeking forgiveness is the repentance of liars, and your repentance needs repentance." He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, what is repentance?" He said: "It is a term that applies to six meanings: for the past sins, regret; for neglecting the obligations, making them up; restoring the rights that were violated; making the soul taste the hardship of obedience as you made it taste the sweetness of disobedience; and weeping in place of every laugh you laughed." And He pardons evil deeds: this means the major sins when repented of, and the minor sins when major sins are avoided. And He knows what you do: it is read with the *ta'* and with the *ya'*. That is, He knows it, so He rewards good deeds and punishes evil deeds.

Wa-yastajību alladhīna āmanū: ﴿And He answers those who believe﴾, meaning: He answers them (yastajību lahum). The lām has been dropped, as it is dropped in His words ﴿and when they measured [out] for them [or weighed for them]﴾ (wa-idhā kālūhum), meaning: He rewards them for their obedience and increases them in reward out of bounty. Or, if they call upon Him, He answers their supplication, gives them what they asked for, and adds to what they sought.

It has also been said that istijāba (answering) is their own action: they respond to Him with obedience when He calls them to it. ﴿And He increases them of His bounty﴾ refers to an increase over their reward.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that this is their action: they answer Him when He calls them.

It is reported from Ibrahim ibn Adham that he was asked: "Why is it that we call upon Him and are not answered?" He said: "Because He called you and you did not answer Him." Then he recited: ﴿And Allah calls to the abode of peace﴾ [10:25], and ﴿And He answers those who believe﴾.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 27:**

*Labaghaw* (لَبَغَوْا) derives from *al-baghy* (البغي), which means injustice (*al-zulm*). That is: they would transgress, this one against that one and that one against this one, because wealth is (what makes people) *mubtara ma'shira* [[The phrase "mubtara ma'shira" in al-Sihah: *al-ashr* means *al-batar* (insolence, exultation). (ʿ)]], and the state of Qarun suffices as a lesson. From this is the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"What I fear most for my community is the splendour of this world and its abundance" [[Al-Tabari related it through the transmission of Sa'id from Qatada, who said: "It has been mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)..." in this form, and added: "It used to be said: the best provision is that which neither makes you transgress nor distracts you." In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, with the wording: "Indeed, what I fear most for you is what will be opened up to you of the splendour of this world."]]. And from one of the Arabs:

*And the rain of al-Wasmi has made grow between us
and between the Banu Rumman, nabiʿ and shawhat*[[It is narrated: "And al-Wasmi has made grow..." where al-Wasmi is the first rain of the year, because it marks (*yasim*) the earth with vegetation. The *nabiʿ* is a tree from which bows are made.

*Al-Shawhat* is similar, meaning: the rain may begin to make trees grow between us and them. The meaning is: they seek to remain (in one place) until the trees between them become large, because they are rich and do not travel much as others do. Or the meaning is: when spring came and those trees matured, they would make spears and bows from them and fight one another. So the verse is a metaphor for the outbreak of war between the two tribes, and this is what the context indicates, as does the mention of "between" and the specification of that particular tree.]]

That is: they came to life and so spoke to themselves of transgression and mutual rivalry. Or (it means) from *al-baghy*, which is arrogance and pride, that is: they would become proud on earth, and do what follows from pride, such as excess and corruption in it. It was also said: it was revealed concerning a group of the People of the Bench (*Ahl al-Suffa*) who wished for abundance of provision and wealth. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: "It was revealed concerning us, for we looked at the wealth of the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and we desired it."

*Biqadarin* (بِقَدَرٍ): by measure, by determination. It is said: *qadarahu qadaran* and *qadaran*.

*Khabirun basir* (خَبِيرٌ بَصِيرٌ): He knows what their circumstances will lead to, so He determines for them what is best for them and closest to unifying their affairs. Thus He makes some poor and some rich, withholds and gives, restricts and expands, as the divine wisdom requires. Had He made all of them rich, they would have transgressed; had He made all of them poor, they would have perished.

If you say: we see people transgressing against one another, some of whom are given abundance and some of whom are withheld from; if those given abundance transgress, why was abundance given to them? And if those withheld from transgress, then transgression can occur without abundance, so why did He make it conditional? I say: there is no doubt that transgression is less with poverty and greater and more prevalent with abundance, and each of these is a clear cause for going forward into transgression or refraining from it. So if abundance were universal, transgression would prevail until the matter is reversed from what it is now [[His words "the reverse of what it is now": perhaps it is "what it is". (ʿ)]].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 42, verse 28:

It is read "qanatu" (they despair) with the nun both vowelled with a fatha and with a kasra. "Wa yanshuru rahmatahu" means: the blessings of the rain, its benefits, and the fertility that results from it. It is related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was told: "The drought has become severe and the people have despaired." He said: "Then they have been given rain." By this he meant this verse. It is also permissible that he meant His mercy in everything, as if He said: He sends down the mercy which is the rain, and spreads other than it of His vast mercy. "Al-Waliyy" is the One who takes charge of His servants with His goodness; "al-Hamid" is the One who is praised for that, and the people of His obedience praise Him for it.

﴿And what He has scattered﴾ may be in the nominative or the genitive, construed as agreeing either with the genitive noun before it or with the noun it is attached to.

If you ask: why is ﴿of living creatures﴾ (min dabbah) used for both of them, when the creatures (ad-dawab) are only on the earth? I answer: it is permissible to attribute a thing to all of what has been mentioned even if it pertains to only part of it, as one says: "The Banu Tamim have among them a skilled poet, or a brave hero," when he is only in a *fakhdh* (a subdivision of a clan) of theirs, or in a *fasila* (a lineage group) of their *fasa'il*, and "The Banu so-and-so did such-and-such," when only one of them did it. From this is His saying ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾, while they come forth only from the salt water. [Footnote: His words "*fakhdh*": the divisions of tribes, the smallest of which is the *fakhdh*, above it the *batn* (sub-clan), then the *'imara*, then the *fasila*, then the *qabila* (tribe), then the *sha'b* (people/nation). The last is the most comprehensive. This is noted in *al-Sihah* (the lexicon of al-Jawhari). (ʿ)]

[Footnote: Mahmud said: "If you ask: why is ﴿of living creatures﴾ used for both of them, when the creatures are on the earth alone? He answered that it is permissible to attribute a thing to all of what has been mentioned even if it belongs to only part of it, like His saying ﴿From both of them come forth pearls and coral﴾, while they come forth only from the salt water..." etc.

Ahmad said: The application of *dawab* (creatures) to humans is far from the usage of the language, so how much more so its application to the angels. The correct view, God knows best, is the first aspect, and it has been explained in more than one verse, such as His saying ﴿Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day...﴾, then He said ﴿and what God sends down from the sky of water, and quickens thereby the earth after its death, and scatters in it of every creature (*min kulli dabbah*)﴾. So He restricted this matter to the earth, God knows best.]

It is possible that the angels, peace be upon them, have a walking as well as flying, so they are described with crawling as humans are described with it. And it is not far-fetched that God creates in the heavens an animal that walks in them as humans walk on the earth. Glory be to the One who created what we know and what we do not know of kinds of creation.

﴿*Idha*﴾ (when) enters upon the present-tense verb just as it enters upon the past tense. God Most High said ﴿By the night when it covers (*idha yaghsha*)﴾, and from it is ﴿when He wills (*idha yasha'*)﴾. The poet said:

"And whenever I wish, I raise from it
at the end of the night, a camel fleeing, frightened."

In the codices of the people of Iraq it reads ﴿فَبِما كَسَبَتْ﴾ (fa-bi-ma kasabat) with the *fa'*, on the basis of imputing to *ma* the meaning of a conditional (*tadmin*, the implicit carrying of a sense from one construction into another). In the codices of the people of Madina it reads ﴿بِما كَسَبَتْ﴾ (bi-ma kasabat) without the *fa'*, on the basis that *ma* is a subject (*mubtada'*) and *bi-ma kasabat* is its predicate, without imputing the meaning of a condition.

The verse is specific to the criminals. [[Mahmud said: "The verse is specific to the criminals..." etc. Ahmad said: In this verse the Qadariyya (the determinists' opponents, here the Mu'tazila who affirm human power over action) are broken, and they cannot devise a stratagem to turn it away from the implication of its wording. They interpreted the words of the Exalted ﴿وَيَغْفِرُ ما دُونَ ذلِكَ لِمَنْ يَشاءُ﴾ (And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills) as referring to the one who repents, but that is not possible for them here, for it has affirmed partiality in forgiveness, and it is impossible in their view that forgiveness here be conjoined with repentance, for that would necessitate that repentance also be partial, and in their view repentance is not divisible. Likewise the Imam transmitted this from Abu Hashim, the head of the Mu'tazila and the one who took the greatest part in it among them. So there is no interpretation for it except the truth about which there is no doubt, namely that forgiveness is returned to the will of Allah the Exalted and is not contingent upon repentance.

As for Zamakhshari's statement that the pains that befall children and the insane have compensations, he means by it that compensation is obligatory upon Allah the Exalted according to the context of his creed, and he has erred in the principle and in the branch. For although the Mu'tazila erred in obligating compensation, they did not hold it obligatory for children and the insane. Do you not see that the Qadi Abu Bakr (al-Baqillani) confronted them with the ugliness of inflicting pain on animals, children and the insane, and said: they have no compensations, and it is not contingent upon a prior entitlement so that it could be good. Thus the confrontation is only completed by their agreement with him that they have no compensations.]] It is not impossible that Allah exacts part of the punishment of the criminal and pardons part of it. As for one who has no crime, like the prophets, children and the insane, if some pain or other befalls them, then it is for the complete compensation and the benefit.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no twitching of a vein, no scratch from a stick, and no stumbling of a stone except because of a sin, and Allah pardons more than that." [[Transmitted by Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim by way of Isma'il ibn Sulaym from al-Hasan, and al-Tabari and al-Bayhaqi at the end of al-Shu'ab, from Qatada; both are mursal (the Companion is omitted from the chain). Abd al-Razzaq connected it through the narration of al-Salt ibn Bahram from Abu Wa'il from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

And from some of them: whoever does not know that what reaches him of trials and calamities is through his own earning, and that what his Master pardons is more, has little regard for the goodness of his Lord towards him. And from another: the servant is constantly bound to offences at every time, and his offences in his acts of obedience are more than his offences in his acts of disobedience, because the offence of disobedience is in one respect and the offence of obedience is in many respects. Allah purifies His servant of his offences by various kinds of calamities, so as to lighten his burdens on the Day of Resurrection, and were it not for His pardon and mercy he would perish at the first step.

And from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), raising it (to the Prophet): "Whoever is pardoned in this world, Allah pardons him in the Hereafter." [[Transmitted by Ibn Majah from the narration of Abu Juhayfa from Ali, raised, with the wording: "Whoever commits a sin in this world and is punished for it, then Allah is too just to repeat His punishment upon a servant.
